title: MARY MAGDALENE WAS NOT CALLED A PROSTITUTE: How Did That Story Become So Popular?
paragraphs:
MARY MAGDALENE WAS NOT CALLED A PROSTITUTE: How Did That Story Become So Popular?
For centuries, millions have pictured Mary Magdalene as the Bible’s redeemed prostitute. There is only one problem: the Gospels never call her one. And what Scripture actually says about Mary may be far more powerful than the story many of us inherited.
There are some things you can hear so many times that eventually you stop asking whether they are actually written in the Bible.
Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
You may have heard it in a sermon.
Seen it in a painting.
Watched it portrayed in a movie.
Perhaps you remember the familiar image: a sexually immoral woman with a scandalous past encounters Jesus, falls at His feet, and becomes one of His devoted followers.
It is certainly a dramatic story of redemption.
There is just one serious problem.
The Bible never tells that story about Mary Magdalene.
Read that again.
Not once in Matthew.
Not once in Mark.
Not once in Luke.
Not once in John.
The New Testament never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute.
It never says she sold her body.
It never identifies sexual immorality as her particular past.
It never even explicitly identifies her as the unnamed “sinful woman” who anointed Jesus in Luke 7.
What Scripture actually tells us is simultaneously more restrained and more extraordinary.
Luke introduces her immediately after the account of that unnamed woman, but he introduces Mary as a named person among the women accompanying Jesus:
“Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils.”
—Luke 8:2, KJV
The Greek is striking:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē, aph’ hēs daimonia hepta exelēlythei.
In straightforward English:
“Mary, the one called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.”
That is what Luke tells us.
Seven demons.
Not seven sexual sins.
Not prostitution.
Not adultery.
Not a career in sexual immorality.
Seven demons had gone out from her.
And we need to resist the temptation to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
Because when God gives us a person’s story, we do not have permission to rewrite the scandal.
And perhaps there is something deeply personal hiding inside that truth.
Because maybe somebody once rewrote yours.
Maybe something happened to you...
and eventually what people said about you became bigger than what actually happened.
A failure became your identity.
A divorce became your identity.
An addiction became your identity.
A season of rebellion became your identity.
A pregnancy became your identity.
A prison sentence became your identity.
A breakdown became your identity.
A rumor became your identity.
Something you did became the permanent headline above your life.
Or perhaps something done to you became the name people quietly attached to you.
And suddenly Mary Magdalene’s story is no longer merely an interesting historical correction.
It becomes painfully familiar.
Because human beings have always been good at turning somebody’s darkest chapter into their permanent biography.
Jesus does something different.
The Gospels do not introduce Mary by giving us lurid details about her bondage.
They introduce us to a woman who had been delivered.
That distinction matters.
Mary Magdalene had known darkness.
Whatever the precise nature and experience of her demonic oppression was—and Scripture does not give us enough information to reconstruct it safely—Luke wants us to know something unmistakable:
Jesus Christ had set her free.
Seven demons had gone out.
And after deliverance came discipleship.
Luke continues by naming Joanna, Susanna, and “many others,” women who accompanied Jesus and the Twelve and helped support the ministry from their resources.
Mary was not merely standing somewhere in the background of Christianity’s story.
She followed Christ.
She served.
She remained.
And when the story became unbearable, she was still there.
Think about that.
When Jesus was crucified, Mary Magdalene appears among the women associated with the crucifixion accounts.
When His body was laid in the tomb, she was there.
When Sabbath darkness gave way to resurrection morning, she went to the tomb.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking encounters in the New Testament.
John 20 places Mary outside the tomb...
weeping.
The Greek verb is κλαίω — klaiō.
She is grieving.
The One who had transformed her life was dead—or so she believed.
Then she sees someone.
She thinks He is the gardener.
Jesus asks why she is crying.
She still does not recognize Him.
And then...
one word.
Her name.
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
“Mary.”
Imagine hearing your name spoken by the Man you watched die.
Imagine grief colliding with impossible hope.
Imagine believing everything was over...
and suddenly discovering that Death itself had lost.
Mary turns toward Him.
“Rabboni!”
Teacher.
The tomb is empty.
Christ is alive.
And Jesus gives this woman a message.
“Go to my brethren...”
Then John records:
“Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord.”
—John 20:18, KJV
Do not race past that sentence.
She had seen the Lord.

The woman later generations would so often remember primarily through a sexualized story the Gospels never actually assign to her is presented in John as a witness proclaiming the risen Christ to His disciples.
The center of Mary Magdalene’s biblical identity is not prostitution.
It is Jesus.
Deliverance.
Discipleship.
The cross.
The empty tomb.
And resurrection testimony.
So how did the prostitute story become so deeply embedded in Christian imagination?
Part of the answer comes from something that happened centuries after the New Testament was written.
Luke 7 tells the story of an unnamed woman described as a sinner who enters the home of Simon the Pharisee. She weeps at Jesus’ feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them.
Luke does not call that woman Mary Magdalene.
Then Luke 8 introduces Mary Magdalene by name.
Elsewhere, John identifies Mary of Bethany—the sister of Martha and Lazarus—in an anointing account.
Over time, these women became intertwined in parts of Western Christian interpretation.

The association became especially influential through Pope Gregory I, Gregory the Great, in the late sixth century, when he treated Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, and Luke’s unnamed sinful woman as the same person.
That interpretive fusion helped shape centuries of Western preaching, painting, literature, and popular imagination.
Eventually, the picture became so familiar that many Christians assumed they had read it directly in Scripture.
But familiarity is not the same thing as biblical accuracy.
And there is another important correction.
Even Luke 7 does not explicitly say that its unnamed “sinful woman” was a prostitute.
The Greek description is:
γυνὴ... ἁμαρτωλός
gynē... hamartōlos
A “woman... who was a sinner.”
The text tells us she had a sinful reputation.
It does not identify prostitution as her occupation.
That conclusion goes beyond what Luke actually says.
And this is where the story should make every Bible-reading Christian uncomfortable in the best possible way.
Because it is possible to defend a story for centuries...
and still need to open the Bible again.
Tradition can be valuable.
Teachers can help us.
Church history matters.
But Christians ultimately must allow Scripture to correct our assumptions.
Even cherished assumptions.
Especially cherished assumptions.
And correcting this misunderstanding does not weaken the Gospel of grace.
It strengthens it.
Because someone might hear that Mary Magdalene was not called a prostitute and wonder:
“But doesn't that ruin the beautiful redemption story?”
No.
Grace does not need an invented sin to become amazing.
Mary needed Jesus.
So do you.
So do I.
The Gospel does not require us to make Mary more sinful so that Christ can appear more merciful.
Scripture has already settled the condition of humanity:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
Mary needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
The unnamed woman of Luke 7 needed grace.
The thief on the cross needed grace.
The apostle Paul needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
Not because every person has committed the same sins...
but because every sinner needs the same Savior.
And perhaps that is why this correction can reach somewhere deeper than historical curiosity.
Somebody reading this has spent years believing that your worst moment is your truest name.
You believe God looks at you and sees the affair.
The addiction.
The abortion.
The pornography.
The lies.
The betrayal.
The bitterness.
The secret nobody knows.
The years you wasted.
The faith you abandoned.
The marriage you damaged.
The person you hurt.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
And shame keeps whispering:
That is who you are.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel never teaches that repentance means pretending sin never happened.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners.
He cleanses sinners.
He reconciles sinners to God.
He gives new life.
He transforms.
He restores.
He makes people His own.
This is why Paul could write:
—2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean sin becomes insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
And grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
That is Christianity.
Not self-improvement.
Not reputation management.
Not pretending darkness never existed.
Death...
then resurrection.
Guilt...
then forgiveness.
Bondage...
then freedom.
Lost...
then found.
Enemy...
then reconciled.
Sinner...
saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Mary Magdalene understood something about deliverance that comfortable religion can easily forget.
When you know what Christ rescued you from, following Him stops feeling like an accessory to your life.
It becomes your life.
And look where Mary eventually stands.
Near the cross.
Near the tomb.
Then before the risen Christ.
That sequence almost preaches by itself.
The cross.
The tomb.
The risen Jesus.
That is where every Christian story ultimately has to go.
Not merely toward Mary.
Toward Christ.
Mary Magdalene matters precisely because Jesus matters infinitely more.
She does not save us.
Her story does not save us.
Correcting misconceptions about her does not save us.
Jesus Christ saves.
The crucified and risen Son of God is the center.
And maybe the most beautiful thing about correcting Mary Magdalene’s story is discovering that the biblical version does not diminish grace at all.
It reveals something about grace we desperately need to remember.
Jesus does not need human beings to exaggerate your darkness in order to demonstrate His light.
He knows exactly what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what was bondage.
He knows what was sin.
He knows what was suffering.
He knows what was rumor.
He knows what was true.
He knows the parts everybody misunderstood.
And He knows the parts nobody knows at all.
There is nowhere to hide from Him.
And there is no reason to manufacture a cleaner biography before coming to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come empty-handed.
Come to Christ.
Maybe your story really is scandalous.
Maybe nobody had to invent anything.
Maybe if everything were projected onto a screen in church next Sunday, you would want the ground to swallow you.
The Gospel is still for sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by your ability to repair your reputation.
It was purchased by His blood.
So repent.
Believe.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ is calling you to abandon.
Stop making peace with chains He came to break.
Stop assuming that because you have failed repeatedly you are beyond the reach of mercy.
Run to Jesus.
The woman standing outside the empty tomb reminds us that Christ can take a human life that has known profound darkness and make that life a witness to resurrection.
That is the heartbeat behind From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not inventing scandals Scripture never recorded.
Not celebrating sin.
But declaring that Jesus Christ has the final word over every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
Send it to the person who has always believed Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
Send it to the person drowning in shame.
Send it to the believer who thinks their past disqualified them forever.
And perhaps send it to someone who does not yet believe at all.
Let them encounter not merely an interesting correction about Mary Magdalene...
but the Jesus who stood outside a tomb alive.
Come back to the Scriptures in it. Test what you have read against the Word of God. Christians should never fear careful examination of Scripture.

Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor and is not a condition of glorifying Him—Christians glorify God through lives of faith, love, obedience, worship, generosity, and service—but if this particular ministry is feeding you spiritually and you want to help it reach others, your support can become part of making that work possible.
Leave looking at Jesus.
The Jesus who delivers.
The Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
The Jesus who went willingly to the cross.
The Jesus whose body was placed inside a tomb.
The Jesus who walked out alive.
The Jesus who called Mary by name.
And the Jesus who still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Mary Magdalene's story was never powerful because later generations could attach a sensational past to her.
It was powerful because Jesus Christ had changed her future.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you tonight:
People may keep introducing you by a chapter Jesus has already turned—but when Christ writes the ending, the tomb does not get the final word.
